text: R packages come three main sources, serving different purposes: CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network): official repository general-purpose R packages. Packages undergo basic quality checks easy install using install.packages(). Bioconductor: specialised repository bioinformatics packages. GitHub: code hosting platform developers share packages may active development yet submitted CRAN/Bioconductor. install using remotes::install_github(). install packages specific order (CRAN → Bioconductor → GitHub) ensure dependencies resolved correctly.

text: Quality control (QC) critical first step single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. goal QC identify remove low-quality cells confound downstream analysis. Poor quality cells can arise several sources: empty droplets contain ambient RNA, dying cells compromised membranes, doublets two cells captured single droplet. module, work single nuclei RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) data human heart tissue. data comes study examining human heart development across three stages: foetal, young, adult (Sim et al., 2021, Circulation). Understanding heart changes cellular level across development provides insights cardiac maturation potential therapeutic targets.

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: Traditional “bulk” RNA-sequencing measures average gene expression across millions cells. powerful, approach masks heterogeneity exists within tissues. Single cell RNA-sequencing overcomes limitation measuring gene expression individual cells, allowing us : Identify distinct cell types within tissue Discover rare cell populations Study cell--cell variability Track cellular states development disease widely used platform scRNA-seq 10X Genomics Chromium system, captures cells oil droplets along barcoded beads. bead carries oligonucleotides three key components: Cell barcode: Identifies cell RNA came Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI): Identifies individual RNA molecules, removing PCR amplification bias Poly-dT tail: Captures polyadenylated mRNA

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: quality control, dataset high-quality cells. However, can identify cell types, must address two important challenges: Technical variation: Raw count data affected differences sequencing depth cells. cell total counts appear higher expression genes, even underlying biology identical. Normalisation removes technical variation. Batch effects: Cells processed different batches (different days, different samples) may show systematic differences unrelated biology. Integration methods correct batch effects preserving true biological variation. module, normalise data using SCTransform, integrate samples using Harmony, identify cell clusters using graph-based clustering. overall workflow follows standard single cell analysis pipeline: step builds upon previous one, progressively transforming data raw gene counts biologically interpretable cell clusters.

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: Normalisation one critical steps single cell analysis. Unlike bulk RNA-seq, samples similar total counts, single cells can vary orders magnitude total UMI counts due differences cell size, RNA content, capture efficiency. SCTransform (Hafemeister & Satija, 2019) uses regularised negative binomial regression normalise UMI count data. approach: Models relationship observed counts sequencing depth gene using negative binomial distribution Computes Pearson residuals represent deviation expected expression given sequencing depth Identifies genes high biological variability (variable features) drive downstream analyses key insight highly expressed genes show variance simply due sampling effects. SCTransform accounts modelling mean-variance relationship, allowing fair comparison across genes different expression levels. vst.flavor = "v2" option uses improved algorithm (Choudhary & Satija, 2022) : Uses geometric mean library size reference (robust) Implements improved regularisation better handling outliers Provides stable results large datasets SCTransform automatically identifies highly variable genes. Let us examine top variable features: can visualise mean-variance relationship:
code: # Run SCTransform normalisation # This may take 1-2 minutes set.seed(42)  # For reproducibility seu <- SCTransform(     seu,     vst.flavor = "v2",     seed.use = 42,     verbose = FALSE ) # Get the top 10 variable features top_features <- head(VariableFeatures(seu), 10) top_features ##  [1] "F13A1"     "NRXN1"     "SLC8A1"    "ACSM3"     "XKR4"      "CNTNAP2"   ##  [7] "LINC02388" "KAZN"      "PKHD1L1"   "NEGR1" # Plot variable features VariableFeaturePlot(seu) +     ggtitle("Variable Features (SCTransform)") +     theme_minimal()

Key concepts: Loadings: contribution gene PC. High loading genes “define” component. Embeddings: coordinates cell PC space. Used downstream analysis. Variance explained: much total variation PC captures. PCA, typically use first 20-50 PCs, capture biological signal discarding noise higher components.
code: # Run PCA on the SCTransform-normalised data # By default, this uses the variable features identified by SCTransform set.seed(42) seu <- RunPCA(seu, seed.use = 42, verbose = FALSE)

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: analysing data multiple samples batches, cells often cluster sample origin rather cell type. happens sample unique technical characteristics (slight differences dissociation, library preparation, sequencing) create systematic biases. Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) fast effective integration method corrects batch effects preserving biological variation. algorithm works follows: Soft clustering: Cells assigned probabilistically multiple clusters PCA space Calculate centroids: cluster, compute centroid separately batch Adjust embeddings: Move cells toward global centroid, removing batch-specific shifts Iterate: Repeat convergence key advantage Harmony operates directly PCA embeddings, making fast memory-efficient. Unlike methods require re-analysis raw counts, Harmony can integrate datasets seconds minutes. Important considerations: -integration: Aggressive correction can merge distinct cell types. check examining marker genes clustering. -integration: Insufficient correction leaves batch effects. verify checking sample mixing UMAP. Biological variation: sample-specific patterns real biology (e.g., disease vs healthy). Harmony preserve removing technical artefacts.
code: # Run Harmony integration # group.by.vars specifies which variable contains batch information # Here we integrate by sample to remove sample-specific technical effects set.seed(42)  # Harmony has stochastic components seu <- RunHarmony(     seu,     group.by.vars = "sample",     reduction.use = "pca",     dims.use = 1:n_dims,     verbose = FALSE )

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: PCA excellent capturing global structure variance, uses linear projections represent complex, non-linear relationships cells. UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation Projection; McInnes et al., 2018) addresses limitation. UMAP works : Building high-dimensional graph: Connect cell nearest neighbours high-dimensional space (Harmony embeddings) Optimising low-dimensional representation: Find 2D coordinates preserve neighbour relationships much possible Key properties UMAP: Local structure preserved: Cells close original space remain close UMAP Global structure approximate: Distances distant groups less meaningful Clusters appear islands: Distinct cell types typically form separate “islands” UMAP space Important caveats: UMAP primarily visualisation, quantitative analysis size density clusters UMAP reflect number cells -interpret distances clusters run UMAP Harmony-corrected embeddings ensure batch effects distort visualisation:
code: set.seed(42)  # UMAP is stochastic - seed ensures reproducible embeddings seu <- RunUMAP(     seu,     reduction = "harmony",     dims = 1:n_dims,     seed.use = 42,     verbose = FALSE )

text: Seurat implements graph-based clustering two steps: Step 1: Build K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) Graph cell connected K nearest neighbours reduced dimensional space (Harmony embeddings). Two cells connected similar gene expression profiles. result graph : Nodes = cells Edges = connections similar cells Edge weights = strength similarity Step 2: Community Detection (Louvain Algorithm) Louvain algorithm identifies “communities” densely connected cells. optimises modularity—measure much densely connected cells within community compared random expectation. algorithm: Starts cell community Iteratively moves cells communities improve modularity Aggregates communities repeats improvement

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: resolution parameter main tuning parameter clustering. controls granularity identified clusters: Lower resolution (0.1-0.3): Produces fewer, larger clusters. Identifies major cell types may merge subtypes. Medium resolution (0.4-0.6): Balances major types subtypes. Often good starting point. Higher resolution (0.8-1.2): Produces , smaller clusters. Can reveal rare subtypes may -split continuous populations. “correct” resolution—appropriate choice depends biological question. interested major cell types, use lower resolution. want identify rare subtypes, use higher resolution. test range resolutions 0.1 1.0 understand clusters behave across resolution spectrum: Let us see many clusters resolution produces:

Epicardial         "UPK3B", "WT1",         # Proliferating         "MKI67", "TOP2A"     ),     celltype = c(         rep("Cardiomyocytes", 9),         rep("Fibroblasts", 7),         rep("Pericytes", 4),         rep("Endothelial", 5),         rep("Smooth Muscle", 4),         rep("Macrophages", 5),         rep("T Cells", 4),         rep("Schwann", 3),         rep("Epicardial", 2),         rep("Proliferating", 2)     ) )  # Define colors for each cell type celltype_colors <- c(     "Cardiomyocytes" = "#D62728",     "Fibroblasts" = "#1F77B4",     "Pericytes" = "#2CA02C",     "Endothelial" = "#9467BD",     "Smooth Muscle" = "#FF7F0E",     "Macrophages" = "#8C564B",     "T Cells" = "#E377C2",     "Schwann" = "#7F7F7F",     "Epicardial" = "#17BECF",     "Proliferating" = "#333333" )  # Filter to available genes marker_info <- marker_info[marker_info$gene %in% rownames(seu), ] marker_genes <- marker_info$gene gene_colors <- celltype_colors[marker_info$celltype] marker_info$celltype_f <- factor(marker_info$celltype, levels = names(celltype_colors))  # Order clusters by cell type identity for diagonal pattern # Preferred order based on cell type (CM, Fibroblasts, Pericytes, Endothelial, Immune, Neural, etc.) preferred_order <- c("0", "6", "8", "17", "7", "9", "2", "11", "15", "1", "12", "3", "5", "13", "18", "4", "14", "16", "10") # Filter to only clusters that exist in our data actual_clusters <- as.character(unique(seu$seurat_clusters)) cluster_order <- preferred_order[preferred_order %in% actual_clusters] # Add any clusters not in preferred order (shouldn't happen, but safety) cluster_order <- c(cluster_order, setdiff(actual_clusters, cluster_order)) seu$cluster_ordered <- factor(seu$seurat_clusters, levels = cluster_order)  # Calculate cell type label positions celltype_positions <- marker_info %>%     mutate(pos = row_number()) %>%     group_by(celltype_f) %>%     summarise(start = min(pos) - 0.5, end = max(pos) + 0.5,               mid = mean(pos), .groups = "drop")  # Create DotPlot with cell type annotations DotPlot(seu, features = marker_genes, group.by = "cluster_ordered") +     RotatedAxis() +     scale_colour_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",                            midpoint = 0, name = "Average\nExpression") +     scale_size_continuous(name = "Percent\nExpressed", range = c(0.5, 6)) +     labs(x = NULL, y = "Cluster",          title = "Cell Type Marker Expression (Sim et al. 2021)") +     theme_bw() +     theme(         plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),         axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 10,                                    color = gene_colors, face = "italic"),         axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12),         axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),         panel.grid.major = element_blank(),         panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),         panel.border = element_rect(color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8),         legend.position = "right",         legend.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),         legend.text = element_text(size = 10),         plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 45, 10)     ) +     # Add cell type color bars     annotate("rect",              xmin = celltype_positions$start, xmax = celltype_positions$end,              ymin = -1.8, ymax = -1.2,              fill = celltype_colors[as.character(celltype_positions$celltype_f)]) +     # Add cell type labels inside bars     annotate("text",              x = celltype_positions$mid, y = -1.5,              label = celltype_positions$celltype_f,              size = 3.5, angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold",              color = "white") +     coord_cartesian(clip = "off", ylim = c(0.5, length(cluster_order) + 0.5))

title: Module 4: Differential Expression Analysis
text: critical pitfall single cell differential expression analysis pseudoreplication: treating cells independent biological replicates . Cells sample share technical biological variation violates independence assumption statistical tests. Consider analogy: want compare heights two populations, measuring person multiple times increase sample size. Similarly, capturing 5,000 cells one individual give us 5,000 independent observations individual’s biology. Many single cell DE methods (Wilcoxon test, t-test, MAST) operate cell level treat cell independent replicate. approaches: Inflate Type error rates (false positives) dramatically Produce artificially small p-values reflect true significance Confound biological technical variation generalise findings beyond specific samples analysed solution pseudobulk analysis: aggregating counts across cells within sample create sample-level expression estimates, applying well-established bulk RNA-seq methods. approach: Correctly identifies biological replicate (sample/individual) Properly controls false discovery rates Accounts sample--sample variation Produces results generalise population
